title: Known Domain Schemas Hidden in Untyped Blobs or Dynamic Keys
pattern: Known, invariant business attributes are stored as arbitrary JSON/BSON, string-keyed maps, or EAV entries to avoid modeling their schema, shifting domain contracts into scattered runtime lookups.
why_bad: Dynamic lookups and parsing lose compile-time guarantees in application code, invite name/type drift, and distribute validation. Persistent schema choices can also weaken database constraints or complicate queries and indexing, depending on the workload and database; poor performance is not inherent to all JSON storage.
detection: In-memory case: core domain fields use raw `serde_json::Value`/BSON or generic maps where their meanings and types are known. Database case: structured persistent business fields are hidden in JSONB/key-value/EAV storage to avoid schema evolution, with code reading or mutating known attributes through string keys (`hashmap.get("user_age")`). A raw metadata field alone is insufficient: establish that it carries known core domain data rather than intentionally arbitrary content.
counterexample: Genuinely user-defined schemas such as custom form builders whose layout is undetermined at compile time; document storage backends, analytics dashboards, or search indexes whose purpose is arbitrary dynamic content; and raw external webhook logs kept for audit/debugging rather than treated as validated domain objects.
fix:
For in-memory models, deserialize and validate incoming data into concrete domain types before business logic uses it. For known persistent attributes, define an appropriate typed database schema/columns and application types, using deliberate migrations and constraints. Retain genuinely dynamic metadata separately. A typed Rust struct does not itself migrate or constrain stored rows, and database columns do not by themselves establish compile-time application safety.
```rust
struct OrderMetadata {
    referral_source: Option<String>,
    campaign_id: Option<u32>,
}
```
source: *Martin Fowler - Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002)*, "Serialized LOB"; *Steve McConnell - Code Complete (2004)*, Chapter 13.; Titus Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* (2020), Chapter 22 ("Large-Scale Changes"); Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 5.; *Domain Modeling made Functional* by Scott Wlaschin (p. 110).
